submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires when the token being read is a gradable, descriptive adjective - a word that states a quality of the thing it modifies ('decent', 'generous', 'relaxed', 'beautiful', 'comfortable', 'licensed', 'educated', 'tired', plus comparatives and superlatives such as 'better', 'stronger', 'simplest') - and the attribution sits on that token, not on the noun after it. It is at or near zero on nouns and proper nouns (all 8 nouns in 'They announced a ___ decision.' measured exactly 0.000, and the scan's confound profile has NOUN 0.5% and PROPN 0.7% active against ADJ 13.2%), on base-form and finite verbs ('the town limit/divide/measure/license/combine the policy' 0.00), on adverbs ('spoke honestly/quickly' 0.00, 'widely' 0.13, 'beautifully' 0.32), and on relational/classifying adjectives that file the noun under a category instead of describing it ('legal', 'political', 'national', 'financial', 'social', 'cultural', 'annual', 'rural', 'medical', 'judicial', 'nuclear', 'digital' 0.00-0.30; only 1 of 38 over the active line in a designed battery and 1 of 16 in natural collocations, the exceptions being 'verbal' 0.60 and 'previous' 0.67, with 'technical' 0.47 just under the line). Its write points at the noun the adjective modifies: zero-ablating the pole moves next-token probability off ' deal', ' tone', ' plan' and ' voice' with KL(clean||ablated) 9.6e-4, below the protocol's lookahead line, and the direct unembedding projection is nearly flat (kurtosis 3.7), so it is a detector, not a predictor. The same adjective is about half as strong predicatively ('the offer was generous' 0.61 vs 'a generous offer' 1.27; attributive above predicative in 8 of 8 natural pairs, by 0.11-1.20). Not covered: very common generic quality words that stay low ('big', 'new', 'old', 'important', 'best' 0.00-0.45), function words and pronouns that reach 0.3-0.6 in some contexts (' the' 0.56-0.75, ' you' 0.62), and single-letter or word-fragment tokens in heavily formatted text ('C' of 'Cynthia', 'J' of 'JUDGE', 'c-fos'), which reach the top of the natural-text tail for reasons this hypothesis does not explain.

rival_explanations: It is a comparative/degree detector rather than a quality detector: it fires on 'better', 'worse', 'more fitting', 'most educated' and 'the better the prognosis' because they mark a comparison, so a plain descriptive adjective with no degree reading should be weak and comparatives of any word class should fire (this rival fits 8 of the scan's top 20 but predicts 'best' and 'worst' weakly, as measured: 0.25 and 0.00).

It is a shape detector for derived adjectival endings - the -ed/-ing participial and -able/-ful/-ous/-ive derivations fire while -al/-ic/-ial words do not - so 'a musical evening', 'a physical reaction' and 'a historical account' should stay at zero even when they plainly describe a quality (in the same frame they measured 0.000, 0.000 and 0.000, which favours this rival over the meaning-based reading).

It is a general pre-head-dependent detector, so determiners, adverbs and pre-verbal pronouns in the same left-of-head slot should fire as strongly as adjectives ('Can you add' 2.01 and 'How can I' 2.16 in the scan, ' the' up to 0.75 in 'to the bench'); the adjective result is then only the largest instance of a broader modifier feature, and the near-zero adverbs I measured are the evidence against it.

Hi all, just found this part of the forum.
I moved to Orlando from Nashville about 5 years ago to attend UCF. I live close to campus and work in Sanford.
Looking forward to future events!
Maybe same plans as PseudoStache suggested?
Unfortunately won't be able to make the 11th. Have fun!
What did you end up deciding about the termite treatment vs termite bond? I checked with some of my neighbors, and no one has a termite bond. One guy has a termite treatment contract. The rest of us just wing it. These are mostly older homes built from 1930's-50's, and no issues so far.
Hi, Roots: Yeah, we landed on winging it, lol. Interesting about the age of the homes you mentioned: my co-worker has a home from that time frame and he said something about how older wood is harder and less likely to get termites. I did two seconds of research and it seems like termites mostly prefer younger wood, which tends to be more moist and, for lack of a better phrase, easier to chew? So sounds like older homes may have a slightly less chance of getting them? At least anecdotally.
Regarding Sunday's meet-up with Pseudostace and maybe Bemly: I'll actually be there at noon for once! Shocking, lol. Am looking forward to ramen. Mmm. It would be nice if it were a tiny bit cold/cozy for the ramen versus this heat wave that seems to be coming through. It's February, for goodness' sake!

It's so nice to see I'm not the only one here in Orlando.

ARCH =		x86
KERNEL =	KraKern

## Compilers
CC =		g++
ASM =		nasm
LD =		ld

## Includes
INCS =	-I includes/boot \
		-I includes/core \
		-I includes/lib \
		-I modules/$(ARCH)/

## Flags
CFLAGS =	-g -O2 -w $(INCS) -trigraphs -fno-builtin \
			-fno-exceptions -fno-stack-protector -O0 \
			-m32 -fno-rtti -nostdlib -nodefaultlibs

LDFLAG =	-melf_i386 -static -L ./ -T ./boot/$(ARCH)/linker.ld --entry=_start 
ASMFLAGS =	-f elf -o

## Versions
VERSION =		1.0
EXTRAVERSION =	dev
SHA =			$(shell git rev-parse --verify HEAD)

include ./boot/$(ARCH)/Makefile
include ./kernel/Makefile
include ./lib/Makefile
include ./modules/$(ARCH)/Makefile

TOTAL=		$(shell echo $(OBJS) | sed 's/ /\n/g' | wc -l)
CURRENT=	01

all: $(KERNEL)

$(KERNEL): $(OBJS)
	@$(LD) $(LDFLAG) -o $@ $^
	@echo "Linking kernel to $@..."
	@echo "Compilation done for $(KERNEL)-$(VERSION)-$(ARCH) ($(SHA))"

%.o: %.cpp
	@$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -DVERSION=\"$(VERSION)\" -DNAME=\"$(KERNEL)\" -DARCH=\"$(ARCH)\" -DEXTRAVERSION=\"$(EXTRAVERSION)\" -DHASH=\"$(SHA)\" -c $< -o $@
	@echo "[$(shell printf "%02d" $(CURRENT))/$(TOTAL)]\tCompiling (C++) $@..."
	$(eval CURRENT=$(shell echo $$(($(CURRENT)+1))))

%.o: %.s
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

%.o: %.asm
	@$(ASM) $(ASMFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
	@echo "[$(shell printf "%02d" $(CURRENT))/$(TOTAL)]\tCompiling (ASM) $@..."
	$(eval CURRENT=$(shell echo $$(($(CURRENT)+1))))

install: $(KERNEL)
	@echo "Installing kernel image..."
	@rm -f kern.img
	@cp clean.img kern.img
	@sudo losetup -o 32256 /dev/loop1 ./kern.img
	@sudo mount /dev/loop1 /mnt
	@sudo cp $(KERNEL) /mnt/boot/.
	@sudo umount /mnt
	@sudo losetup -d /dev/loop1
	@echo "Launching KVM..."
	@./qemu.sh

clean:
	@rm -f $(OBJS)
	@echo "Cleaning objects..."

fclean: clean
	@rm -f $(KERNEL)
	@echo "Cleaning Kernel..."

re: fclean all

The term "international organization" includes intergovernmental organizations (IGOs), international nongovernmental organizations (INGOs), and supranational organizations. The following chart highlights the distinctions between these three types of organizations:
|Intergovernmental Organizations (IGOs)||
IGOs are composed predominantly of states, established by a treaty or other instrument of international law, and possess autonomous organs with a will separate from its individual members. They exist for a variety of purposes, including regional cooperation (ASEAN), security alliances (NATO), or dedcation to a particular purpose (WTO).
|UN, ASEAN, Council of Europe, WTO|
|International Nongovernmental Organizations (INGOs)||Generally private, voluntary organizations whose members are individuals or associations that come together to achieve a common purpose. NGOs can be funded privately or through partial government funds.||Amnesty International, OXFAM, Doctors Without Borders|
|Supranational Organizations||An international organization with "supranational powers" is capable of binding member states to its decisions and laws. Thus, these organizations often have more governmental authority and law-making power than traditional international organizations.||European Union|
This Section will provide a brief overview of four major IGOs, including two regional organizations (ASEAN and Council of Europe), the United Nations, and the World Trade Organization. For more information on specific INGOs, run a Google search for the organization and visit their website.
The European Union is a supranational organization, which means that its member states are bound by the laws, regulations, and judicial decisions of the organization. This type of organization stands in contrast to other, traditional international organizations that typically do not carry governmental and law-making authority. The European Union is not specifically addressed in this research guide.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The political committee filed its annual financial report on Tuesday morning, before the hearing began.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Relational and classifying adjectives the hypothesis lists as inert ('political', 'annual', 'financial') sit attributively with no descriptive adjective anywhere in the sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The town council voted to limit the measure and divide the budget next spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Base-form verbs used exactly as the hypothesis's own zero case ('limit', 'divide') take noun objects ('measure', 'budget'), so the claimed feature is absent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She spoke honestly about the delay and answered every question quickly before the break.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Manner adverbs ('honestly', 'quickly') that the hypothesis reports at 0.00 appear after finite verbs, with no gradable descriptive adjective.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The medical staff reviewed the social and cultural impact of the federal policy.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Four relational adjectives from the hypothesis's inert list are used attributively, testing whether the relational class really stays below the line.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They dug a well behind the barn and covered it with boards before winter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'well' occurs only as a common noun, the part-of-speech shift of a token that peaks as an adverb in the scan.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He knew better than to argue with the inspector about the fence by the road.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'better' is tagged ADV in the fixed idiom 'knew better than', where it names no quality of a modified noun and falls in the hypothesis's adverb zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She did her best to fix the pipes before the guests arrived for dinner.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'best' is the common superlative the hypothesis reports staying at 0.00-0.45, in a frame where it names no quality of a following noun.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The city licensed the vendor last year and renewed the permit in May.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'licensed' is a finite past-tense verb, not an attributive adjective, so the hypothesis predicts its stated finite-verb zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They tired of the argument and left the meeting before the vote.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'tired' is a finite verb governing 'of the argument', not the descriptive participle the hypothesis counts as activating.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The manager relaxed the rules during the holiday week and nobody in the office complained.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'relaxed' is a finite verb governing 'the rules', not an adjective stating a quality of a thing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The crew optimized the route last month and cut the fuel bill for the store.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'optimized' is a past-tense verb, testing a claimed trigger token in the finite-verb sense the hypothesis scores at zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The campaign educated voters about the ballot rules over the summer and into the autumn.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'educated' is a finite verb with an object, not an attributive adjective such as 'an educated guess'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Can you add the two figures on page four and send me the total?
adversarial_test_results.detail: Pre-verbal pronoun and determiner in the exact frame the scan peaked on ('Can you add'), with no adjective in the sentence at all.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The plan could well have been in place before the winter set in.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'well' is a degree adverb inside a modal perfect, so the hypothesis's adverb zero predicts nothing while a degree detector should fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The delegation met Marcus at the station in Denver on Friday and said nothing.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Proper nouns ('Marcus', 'Denver', 'Friday') that the hypothesis reports at 0.7%, with no descriptive adjective present.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The hall held more people than we expected, and some stood at the back.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Comparative determiner 'more' marks a comparison of quantity but describes no modified thing, which the hypothesis's adjective-only reading excludes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She ran faster after the coach changed her stride and her breathing on the track.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Comparative adverb 'faster', excluded by the hypothesis's adverb and adjective restriction but included by a comparative-of-any-class reading.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The meetings, notes, decisions and paperwork filled the week before the recess.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare plural nouns dominate and no adjective appears, testing the hypothesis's noun class while the pre-head-dependent rival can only point at the determiner 'the'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The shop on the corner sells tools as well as garden supplies and paint.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'well' is fixed inside the compound preposition 'as well as', so it is neither the adjective nor the degree adverb either rival would need.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The plant supplies nuclear power to a digital network across rural counties.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Three relational adjectives ('nuclear', 'digital', 'rural') in ordinary attributive use, the class the hypothesis lists as inert.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The group crossed a narrow bridge over a steep ravine before dusk fell.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Plain gradable descriptive adjectives ('narrow', 'steep') with no derived ending and no degree marking, which the hypothesis but not the shape rival should fire on.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The violinist gave an exceptional performance that the critics praised for weeks.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Gradable descriptive adjective ending in '-al' ('exceptional'), which the hypothesis counts as descriptive but the shape rival excludes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her original design won an award at the regional fair in early September.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Another '-al' descriptive adjective ('original') in a novel context, separating the meaning-based reading from the ending-based one.

readings.explanation: The pole fires when the token being read is a gradable, descriptive adjective - a word that states a quality of the thing it modifies ('decent', 'generous', 'relaxed', 'beautiful', 'comfortable', 'licensed', 'educated', 'tired', plus comparatives and superlatives such as 'better', 'stronger', 'simplest') - and the attribution sits on that token, not on the noun after it. It is at or near zero on nouns and proper nouns (all 8 nouns in 'They announced a ___ decision.' measured exactly 0.000, and the scan's confound profile has NOUN 0.5% and PROPN 0.7% active against ADJ 13.2%), on base-form and finite verbs ('the town limit/divide/measure/license/combine the policy' 0.00), on adverbs ('spoke honestly/quickly' 0.00, 'widely' 0.13, 'beautifully' 0.32), and on relational/classifying adjectives that file the noun under a category instead of describing it ('legal', 'political', 'national', 'financial', 'social', 'cultural', 'annual', 'rural', 'medical', 'judicial', 'nuclear', 'digital' 0.00-0.30; only 1 of 38 over the active line in a designed battery and 1 of 16 in natural collocations, the exceptions being 'verbal' 0.60 and 'previous' 0.67, with 'technical' 0.47 just under the line). Its write points at the noun the adjective modifies: zero-ablating the pole moves next-token probability off ' deal', ' tone', ' plan' and ' voice' with KL(clean||ablated) 9.6e-4, below the protocol's lookahead line, and the direct unembedding projection is nearly flat (kurtosis 3.7), so it is a detector, not a predictor. The same adjective is about half as strong predicatively ('the offer was generous' 0.61 vs 'a generous offer' 1.27; attributive above predicative in 8 of 8 natural pairs, by 0.11-1.20). Not covered: very common generic quality words that stay low ('big', 'new', 'old', 'important', 'best' 0.00-0.45), function words and pronouns that reach 0.3-0.6 in some contexts (' the' 0.56-0.75, ' you' 0.62), and single-letter or word-fragment tokens in heavily formatted text ('C' of 'Cynthia', 'J' of 'JUDGE', 'c-fos'), which reach the top of the natural-text tail for reasons this hypothesis does not explain.

It is a comparative/degree detector rather than a quality detector: it fires on 'better', 'worse', 'more fitting', 'most educated' and 'the better the prognosis' because they mark a comparison, so a plain descriptive adjective with no degree reading should be weak and comparatives of any word class should fire (this rival fits 8 of the scan's top 20 but predicts 'best' and 'worst' weakly, as measured: 0.25 and 0.00).

It is a shape detector for derived adjectival endings - the -ed/-ing participial and -able/-ful/-ous/-ive derivations fire while -al/-ic/-ial words do not - so 'a musical evening', 'a physical reaction' and 'a historical account' should stay at zero even when they plainly describe a quality (in the same frame they measured 0.000, 0.000 and 0.000, which favours this rival over the meaning-based reading).

It is a general pre-head-dependent detector, so determiners, adverbs and pre-verbal pronouns in the same left-of-head slot should fire as strongly as adjectives ('Can you add' 2.01 and 'How can I' 2.16 in the scan, ' the' up to 0.75 in 'to the bench'); the adjective result is then only the largest instance of a broader modifier feature, and the near-zero adverbs I measured are the evidence against it.
